Consort

kun-SORT (verb) -- shares a root with 'consortium,' meaning to share a common lot. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To consort to associate with another person repeatedly, often with a hint of disapproval.

Neighbors grew suspicious once they noticed the missing teenager had begun to consort with known car thieves.

Worked Example

A city official is photographed at three different late-night dinners with a contractor under federal investigation, despite claiming in public that he barely knows the man.

That repeated, questionable association is exactly what it means to consort with someone. Unlike 'meet,' which can be a single, innocent encounter, consort implies an ongoing, often suspicious connection.

How Strong Is It? — associate → consort → fraternize

associate vs. consort

associate vs. consort: Associate is a more neutral word than consort -- associate simply means spending time with someone, while consort often carries a hint that the company is questionable.

fraternize vs. consort

fraternize vs. consort: Fraternize can feel more pointed than consort in certain settings: consort broadly implies repeated, often suspicious company, while fraternize is used specifically when mixing with someone crosses a rule or expectation, as in fraternizing with a rival.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — con-

prefix — con-: with, together (Latin)

root — -sort-/-sors-

root — -sort-/-sors-: lot, fate, share (Latin (sors))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin consors meant 'sharing a lot or fate with someone,' from con- ('with') and sors ('lot, share'). To consort with someone, at its root, is to share company and circumstance with them -- the same root that gives us consortium.

Use the root in a new word: consortium

Use the root in a new word: consortium: Five universities formed a consortium to share the cost of the new research telescope.

Word Choice

Consort almost always appears with 'with,' as in 'consort with criminals,' and often carries a disapproving tone about the company someone keeps -- this unit teaches only the verb, not the unrelated noun 'consort' (a monarch's spouse).
